title: ROM, Strength and Function: Turning Measurements into Clinical Decisions
excerpt: A practical framework for selecting, interpreting and communicating range-of-motion, strength and functional measures without mistaking a score for a diagnosis.
seoTitle: ROM, Strength and Functional Assessment | Clinova
seoDescription: Learn how physiotherapists can link ROM, strength and functional testing to patient goals, safety, clinical reasoning and meaningful reassessment.

sections.heading: Start with the person and the task
paragraphs: A useful examination begins before the goniometer or dynamometer. Clarify what the person wants to do, what has changed, the time course, irritability, relevant health conditions, medication, work or caring demands, and what they fear. A shoulder flexion value matters differently to a person reaching a high shelf, dressing, or returning to swimming. The same applies to quadriceps strength when the priority is rising from a low chair, negotiating stairs, or protecting a knee after surgery. A short systems review can reveal cardiopulmonary, neurological, skin, or general-health issues that change the safety of testing. The NHS describes first physiotherapy assessment as including symptoms, history and lifestyle, with checks such as strength and balance; that broad frame is more defensible than an isolated impairment checklist. This educational draft supports professional reflection; it does not confer competency, replace supervision, or supersede local policy, law, referral pathways, or current clinical guidance.

A measurement is a sample of performance under particular instructions, position, effort, pain and equipment conditions. Record those conditions so that a future value is comparable. Consider consent, privacy, communication needs, fatigue and whether an interpreter or supporter is needed. Explain what you will do, why it is relevant, what discomfort might occur and how the person can stop. Consent is an ongoing conversation, not a signature.

sections.heading: Range of motion: describe, do not over-interpret
paragraphs: Decide whether you need active motion, passive motion, or both. Active movement shows available movement plus confidence, motor control, strength and symptom response; passive movement explores what is available when effort and control are reduced, but it is not a pure measure of joint structure. Use consistent landmarks and a named instrument where appropriate. Document side, plane, starting position, end point, symptom behaviour, quality, repetitions and whether the limitation is pain, stiffness, apprehension, weakness or coordination. A difference between active and passive motion can generate a hypothesis, not prove a tissue lesion.

Avoid treating a normative range as a compulsory target. Age, occupation, previous injury, hypermobility, swelling, neurological status and measurement error affect what is meaningful. A small change may be noise; a modest change may be functionally important if it enables a chosen task. Reassess with the same method where possible, but also ask whether the person can now complete the activity that matters. If motion is unexpectedly restricted, rapidly worsening, associated with trauma, systemic symptoms or neurological change, pause and follow local escalation guidance rather than pressing on with testing.

sections.heading: Strength: match the test to the question
paragraphs: Strength testing can range from observation of a task to manual resistance, handheld dynamometry or a validated performance measure. Select the least burdensome method that answers the clinical question. A chair-rise may be more relevant than isolated knee extension for someone struggling at home; a controlled isometric test may be safer when a joint is irritable. State position, lever arm, resistance, effort, pain, repetitions and assistance. Distinguish force production from endurance, power, motor control and willingness to load. A low result may reflect pain inhibition, fear, fatigue, poor leverage, comprehension or neurological deficit; it should not automatically be labelled deconditioning.

Compare sides only when comparison is clinically sensible. The unaffected side may also be impaired, and symmetry is not a universal goal. Standardized outcome measures can make change visible, but their psychometric properties and population fit matter. A test selected because it is familiar is not necessarily the best test. Stop or modify testing for escalating pain, dizziness, unusual breathlessness, new neurological symptoms, loss of balance or signs of medical instability. Use guarding and an appropriate environment when falls or collapse are plausible.

sections.heading: Function is the bridge to participation
paragraphs: Functional assessment asks how impairments interact with real activities: sit-to-stand, reaching, walking, stairs, lifting, transfers, balance or a work-specific task. Observe quality and strategy as well as completion: speed, variability, compensations, symptom response, confidence, cognition, environment and need for equipment or another person. Ask the person to identify which part is difficult and whether the observed task resembles home or work. A performance measure and a patient-reported measure often complement each other: one shows what happened under test conditions; the other captures lived difficulty, priorities and confidence.

Use a standardized tool when its construct, burden, language and measurement properties fit the person and purpose. Record the exact version, score, assistance, timing and context. Do not infer that a better score means tissue healing or that a stable score means no benefit; participation, self-management and safety may improve first. For children or people with communication or cognitive differences, adapt instructions and assess meaningful routines in natural environments when appropriate.

sections.heading: Interpret, plan and reassess
paragraphs: Bring findings together in a transparent clinical hypothesis: what limits the activity, what may be modifiable, what remains uncertain, and what would change your plan. Set goals in the person's language and agree an outcome that can be revisited. A defensible record links baseline findings to the intervention and states how risk was managed. APTA documentation guidance similarly frames tests as hypothesis-driven, emphasizes relevant standardized measures, and warns that a broad disability tool can miss the task most important to an individual.

At review, repeat only measures that can answer the review question. Explain whether change is beyond expected measurement variation when that information is available, while acknowledging uncertainty. If progress is absent, reconsider the working hypothesis, adherence barriers, dosage, context, diagnosis and need for another professional. Escalate when findings exceed scope or suggest serious pathology. This framework is a learning aid, not a protocol: local pathways, professional standards and the person's preferences remain decisive.

takeaways: Select ROM, strength and function measures to answer a person-centred question.
Record test conditions, symptoms, assistance and safety so results are interpretable.
Use scores to inform hypotheses and reassessment, not to make unsupported diagnoses.
Refer or escalate when findings are unexpected, unsafe or outside scope.

references.title: Considerations and Practical Options for Measuring Muscle Strength: A Narrative Review

title: Gait Observation as Clinical Reasoning, Not a Parade of Deviations
excerpt: How to observe walking safely, form testable hypotheses and connect gait findings with function, context and patient priorities.
seoTitle: Gait Observation and Clinical Reasoning | Clinova
seoDescription: A structured guide to safe gait observation, hypothesis testing, functional context, communication and referral in physiotherapy practice.

sections.heading: Define the walking question
paragraphs: Gait observation is most useful when it answers a question. Is the person safe enough to walk? What limits distance, speed or confidence? Which phase or task matters to them? Is a new change associated with pain, weakness, balance, sensory loss, breathlessness, medication or environment? Begin with history and consent, including falls, near misses, footwear, dizziness and the person's own description. Agree where and how to observe, check the route, and have a plan for support. Do not ask someone to demonstrate a risky task solely to complete a form. Walking is not a single laboratory pattern: surface, speed, fatigue, attention, dual task, footwear and fear alter performance.

APTA's examination framework includes balance, gait, locomotion, transfers and transitions as neuromuscular performance, alongside communication, cognition and movement. That breadth guards against reducing gait to ankle angles. Observe in a context resembling the person's goal when safe, while making conditions explicit. A recording is optional: if video is considered, obtain consent, protect privacy and offer a non-recorded alternative. This educational draft supports reflection; it does not confer competency or replace local guidance and supervision.

sections.heading: Observe systematically
paragraphs: Use a consistent sequence: approach and initiation, step and stance symmetry, foot clearance, base of support, trunk and arm strategy, turning, stopping, transfers and recovery. Note speed, cadence, distance and variability if measured; otherwise describe rather than invent precision. Look for what changes with a cue or altered task, but avoid excessive cueing that makes the observation unlike everyday walking. Ask about symptom onset and recovery, and monitor exertion, colour, breathing, dizziness and confidence. Document assistance and guarding using shared local meanings.

Avoid loaded labels such as abnormal without describing the feature. ‘Shorter left step with reduced clearance during fatigue’ is more useful than ‘pathological gait’. A wide base, reduced stance time or slow turning may be an adaptation, a response to pain, or a sign requiring further assessment. A single visual observation has limited reliability and cannot establish causation. Use plain language when sharing it with the person.

sections.heading: Move from pattern to hypothesis
paragraphs: A gait feature is an observation, not a diagnosis. Reduced stance time may reflect pain, fear, weakness or a strategy to avoid loading; foot clearance may involve strength, sensation, coordination, footwear or attention. Generate several plausible explanations and select low-risk tests that discriminate between them: a brief strength or ROM check, sensory screen, sit-to-stand, turning, symptom-linked repeat or medication review. Do not perform a provocative test merely to confirm a favourite theory.

Interpret the whole person. Medication changes, infection, cardiopulmonary disease, orthostatic symptoms, visual impairment, cognition and home hazards may be more important than a biomechanical deviation. When the pattern is new, rapidly progressive, accompanied by falls, syncope, acute neurological signs, severe systemic symptoms or inability to weight bear, stop routine testing and follow urgent local pathways. Referral is a safety action, not an admission of failure.

sections.heading: Test function and capacity
paragraphs: Pair observation with a task measure appropriate to the goal: timed walking, repeated chair-rise, stairs, turning, a validated balance test or a patient-reported mobility measure. Standardize instructions and record aid, footwear, surface, assistance, pain, fatigue and stopping reason. A timed result is not a complete account of participation. Ask how the person manages outdoors, at night, on public transport or while carrying objects, and what they avoid. Repeat at a meaningful interval and examine safety, confidence and activity, not only speed.

If an aid is indicated, assessment includes fit, technique, environment, maintenance and ability to use it, not simply issuing equipment. Involve occupational therapy, nursing, orthotics, medical or falls services when the problem crosses boundaries. For children or people with cognitive or communication differences, adapt instructions and consider meaningful routines in natural settings when appropriate. Record the person's priorities so a technically improved pattern does not eclipse a valued activity.

sections.heading: Communicate the reasoning
paragraphs: Share observations in plain language and check interpretation. Explain uncertainty: ‘I noticed your foot clearance reduced when you tired; I want to understand whether strength, sensation, medication or fatigue contributes.’ Agree what to monitor, what action to take and when to review. Safety-netting should name symptoms that warrant prompt help rather than leave vague reassurance. NICE guidance emphasizes applying recommendations with individual needs, preferences and values, not mechanically.

The aim of gait assessment is safe, meaningful participation, not a cosmetically tidy pattern. Document the reasoning, conditions, assistance, response and plan. Remain within competence, follow local falls and referral pathways, and escalate when risk changes. These notes are educational only and do not supersede current professional standards, emergency advice, or local policy.

sections.heading: Further practice considerations
paragraphs: Context matters: observe lighting, floor transitions, urgency, carrying and divided attention when relevant. Compare performance with baseline rather than an imagined ideal, and describe variability without pathologising it. Link any intervention to a meaningful task, agree challenge and recovery rules, and record response. If fear of falling is present, acknowledge it and use graded support rather than treating fear as non-compliance.

takeaways: Start with a functional question and a safe observation plan.
Describe gait features precisely; treat them as hypotheses, not diagnoses.
Account for fatigue, context, cognition, medication and environment.
Escalate new or progressive changes, falls, syncope or neurological/systemic signs.

title: Evidence-Based Physiotherapy: Integrating Research, Expertise and What Matters to the Person
excerpt: A practical account of evidence-based practice as a cycle of questions, appraisal, shared decisions, implementation and review.
seoDescription: Understand how physiotherapists integrate research evidence, clinical expertise, patient values, safety, uncertainty and local guidance.

sections.heading: Evidence-based practice is integration
paragraphs: Evidence-based practice is not uncritical application of the newest paper or a search for one universally best exercise. It integrates the best available research with professional expertise, the person's goals, preferences, circumstances and risks. NICE says recommendations should be considered alongside individual needs, preferences and values and do not remove professional responsibility. Start by translating uncertainty into a focused question: population, problem, intervention, comparator, outcome and time frame. A question about walking confidence differs from one about pain at rest.

Decide what outcome matters and what harm or burden must be avoided. If the answer is unknown, say so; uncertainty communicated honestly is safer than confident speculation. This educational draft supports professional reflection and does not confer competency, replace supervision, or supersede local policy, law or current guidance.

sections.heading: Find and appraise the right evidence
paragraphs: Match study design to question. Reviews and guidelines may synthesize treatment effects, but inspect currency, eligibility and applicability. Diagnostic questions require attention to reference standards and spectrum; prognosis requires follow-up and missing data; qualitative work can illuminate experience and acceptability. Read beyond an abstract: examine effect size, precision, risk of bias, adverse events, adherence, comparator and whether participants resemble the person in front of you.

A statistically significant average difference may be too small to matter, while a modest average effect may be valuable to someone with few alternatives. Consider absolute effects, confidence intervals and minimal important change where established. Do not convert association into causation or mechanism into outcome evidence. Peer-reviewed evidence is one input; local equipment, safeguarding and service constraints also shape a safe plan.

sections.heading: Apply with clinical reasoning
paragraphs: Clinical expertise helps judge whether an intervention is feasible, safe and adaptable. It includes recognizing contraindications, monitoring response, modifying dosage and knowing when another professional is needed. Expertise is not a licence for preference to outrank evidence; it is the skill of applying evidence to a different person without hiding the mismatch. Document rationale, expected benefit, material risks, alternatives and review triggers.

Shared decision making is more than offering a menu. Explain options in balanced language, including no change or watchful waiting when appropriate, and invite values, constraints and previous experience. Check understanding with teach-back. Accessibility matters: language, hearing, vision, cognition, culture, digital access and health literacy can change whether an evidence-supported plan is usable.

sections.heading: Implement, measure and learn
paragraphs: Implementation turns a recommendation into a workable routine. Co-design dose, timing, prompts, transport, equipment and support. Agree a small set of outcomes: a task, symptom impact, confidence, participation or adverse effect. Review at a planned point and record adherence without moral judgement; non-adherence may signal excessive burden, low confidence, pain flare or structural barriers.

If outcomes disappoint, ask whether intervention delivery, outcome choice, initial hypothesis or context was the issue. Use audit, peer discussion and supervision rather than memory. APTA documentation guidance emphasizes measures with sound psychometric properties and close fit to the person or population. That principle applies to service evaluation as well as individual care.

sections.heading: Know the limits
paragraphs: Evidence can be indirect, incomplete, contradictory or slow to reflect practice. A guideline may be current yet not cover complex comorbidity; a trial may exclude people a service mainly sees. State limitations, seek advice and escalate when the decision exceeds scope. HCPC standards require practice within knowledge and skills, continuing development and referral when needs are beyond scope.

Revisit sources because recommendations change. The quality of reasoning is shown not by certainty, but by a traceable link between question, evidence, person, decision, monitoring and learning. This is a framework, not a treatment recipe or academy claim. Use current national guidance, local pathways, supervision, consent and risk procedures.

sections.heading: Further practice considerations
paragraphs: A transparent evidence search is proportionate to the decision. Record currency, applicability, harms and unresolved questions. Equity matters because trials may exclude people by age, disability, language or socioeconomic circumstance. Ask who can access the intervention and who bears its burden; adapt delivery, monitor outcomes and state uncertainty rather than implying certainty.

A transparent evidence search is proportionate to the decision. Record currency, applicability, harms and unresolved questions. Equity matters because trials may exclude people by age, disability, language or socioeconomic circumstance. Ask who can access the intervention and who bears its burden; adapt delivery, monitor outcomes and state uncertainty rather than implying certainty.

When evidence conflicts, make the disagreement visible. Explain whether uncertainty concerns the size of benefit, who benefits, duration, harms or feasibility. Invite the person to decide what trade-offs are acceptable and agree a review point. Clinical reasoning should remain revisable: a response that differs from expectation is information, not a reason to force the original theory. Discuss difficult decisions with a supervisor or multidisciplinary colleague and record the advice received.

A practical appraisal also asks how the evidence was produced. Consider whether participants received co-interventions, whether outcomes were measured beyond the immediate treatment period, and whether attrition could change the result. Check whether the comparator reflects usual care rather than an inactive ideal. For guidelines, inspect the recommendation strength, evidence certainty, conflicts of interest and update history. When applying a recommendation to a person with multimorbidity, consider interactions, treatment burden and competing goals. A plan can be evidence-informed while remaining individualized, provided the adaptation and its rationale are explicit.

takeaways: Use research, expertise and patient values together; none is sufficient alone.
Appraise applicability, effect size, uncertainty, burden and harms—not just significance.
Co-design an implementable plan with measurable outcomes and review triggers.
Be explicit about evidence limits and remain within scope.

title: Patient Safety, Red Flags and Referral: Managing Uncertainty Responsibly
excerpt: A safety-first approach to screening, escalation, safety netting and referral without overclaiming what red flags can diagnose.
seoTitle: Patient Safety, Red Flags and Referral | Clinova
seoDescription: Learn how to combine history, examination, risk management and safety-netting when serious pathology or care beyond scope is possible.

sections.heading: Safety is a process
paragraphs: Patient safety is more than avoiding a dramatic error. It includes anticipating falls, infection risks, equipment problems, communication gaps, missed deterioration and near misses. A peer-reviewed physiotherapy safety editorial describes safety as a system responsibility and highlights teamwork, effective communication, risk management, human factors and learning from adverse events. Before examination, check identity, environment, consent, equipment, infection precautions, assistance and the person's ability to stop.

Risk is dynamic. Recheck when symptoms, medication, cognition, mobility, vital signs, environment or treatment changes. Do not assume a familiar intervention is harmless: loading, transfers, manual techniques and advice can all create risk in the wrong context. Use local incident, escalation and emergency procedures, and report concerns promptly. This educational draft does not confer competency or replace local policy, law, supervision or emergency advice.

sections.heading: Red flags raise suspicion
paragraphs: Red flags are features that increase concern for serious disease; they are not diagnoses and are not all equally informative. The international IFOMPT framework notes that many commonly listed red flags have limited evidence, few are useful alone, and combinations interpreted with thorough history and examination are more informative. Consider age, health conditions, cancer or infection risk, trauma, immunosuppression, neurological change, systemic symptoms and trajectory rather than ticking a disconnected list.

A negative screen is not a guarantee. A concerning feature does not identify a specific condition. Ask focused follow-up questions, explain why you are concerned, and avoid alarming language or false reassurance. If suspicion rises, stop inappropriate testing and contact the responsible clinician or emergency pathway. Referral urgency depends on presentation and local policy; published frameworks' same-day and urgent examples are guides, not universal rules.

sections.heading: Safety net clearly
paragraphs: Safety netting is an active plan: what to watch for, what action to take, how soon, and who to contact if the plan fails. Use plain language and ask the person to repeat the plan. Include deterioration, new weakness or sensory change, collapse, fever or unexplained systemic change only when relevant; an indiscriminate list obscures the key message. Give written information in an accessible format when appropriate.

Document advice, understanding, timeframe and barriers such as transport, language, health literacy or lack of support. If referral is declined, explore why, explain possible consequences without coercion, assess capacity under applicable law and policy, and record the discussion. Revisit the plan if symptoms evolve. A safety net is not reassurance; it is a shared contingency plan.

sections.heading: Refer within and beyond scope
paragraphs: HCPC standards require practitioners to work only where they have knowledge, skills and experience to meet needs safely and effectively, and to refer when needs exceed scope. Referral is a safety intervention. Identify the recipient, communicate relevant findings, urgency and action already taken, and confirm handover through local process. Involve the wider team when mobility, cognition, safeguarding, medication, mental health, cardiopulmonary or social risks are material.

Avoid using referral as a substitute for reasoning. State the question: urgent medical assessment of neurological signs; review of unexplained systemic symptoms; assessment of falls risk; or advice on medication-related dizziness. Continue only care that is safe while awaiting review, and make ownership clear. If access fails, escalate rather than assume the message was received.

sections.heading: Close the safety loop
paragraphs: A safe record shows concern, evidence, action, recipient, timeframe and follow-up. Share relevant information lawfully and proportionately. HCPC standards require reporting safety concerns and being open when things go wrong. If an incident occurs, provide immediate care, notify the appropriate service, document facts, preserve confidentiality and follow duty-of-candour and local reporting requirements.

Red-flag evidence is evolving, and no checklist confers competence. Use supervision, current guidance and multidisciplinary advice. The goal is not to eliminate uncertainty, an impossible promise, but to recognize when uncertainty itself requires a safer route, a second opinion or closer review. Local referral pathways always govern the action.

sections.heading: Further practice considerations
paragraphs: Screening should be proportionate and revisited, not a ritual checklist. Ask targeted questions about onset, progression, trauma, systemic health, neurological function, medication and exposures, then examine within safe limits. Explain that referral reflects a need for assessment, not a diagnosis. Make urgent action and timeframe unmistakable, and reconcile new information with rehabilitation after review.

Screening should be proportionate and revisited, not a ritual checklist. Ask targeted questions about onset, progression, trauma, systemic health, neurological function, medication and exposures, then examine within safe limits. Explain that referral reflects a need for assessment, not a diagnosis. Make urgent action and timeframe unmistakable, and reconcile new information with rehabilitation after review.

Safety is also relational. People may minimise symptoms because they fear dismissal, cost, stigma or loss of independence. Ask what concerns them and what would make seeking help possible. Respect autonomy while being clear about immediate risk. Where safeguarding, capacity or public-safety duties apply, follow the relevant legal and organisational process and share only proportionate information. Never promise confidentiality that cannot be maintained.

Risk communication should be proportionate. Explain the reason for concern, the uncertainty, and the benefit of prompt review without presenting worst-case possibilities as likely. Ask the person to describe the plan in their own words and identify practical barriers to following it. Consider whether a carer or community team needs to know about mobility assistance, supervision or equipment. If an emergency route is advised, do not leave the person to arrange it alone when their condition or capacity makes that unsafe; follow local escalation policy and document who accepted responsibility.

takeaways: Use red flags as contextual prompts that raise suspicion, not diagnostic tests.
Combine history, examination, trajectory and determinants of health.
Safety-net with specific symptoms, actions, timeframes and accessible communication.
Refer promptly when risk exceeds scope, and close the handover loop.

title: Clinical Documentation and Patient Communication: Making Care Understandable and Traceable
excerpt: Principles for records and conversations that support consent, continuity, shared decisions, safety and professional accountability.
seoTitle: Clinical Documentation and Patient Communication | Clinova
seoDescription: Build clearer physiotherapy records and conversations through consent, plain language, reasoning, safety-netting and accurate handover.

sections.heading: The record is part of care
paragraphs: A clinical record is not a transcript of everything said. It is a contemporaneous, accurate account that enables continuity, supports understanding and makes reasoning reviewable. Start with concerns, relevant history, goals, examination findings, risks, consent, working hypothesis, options, agreed plan and follow-up. Record what was observed, what was reported and what you inferred; keep those categories distinct.

HCPC standards require full, clear and accurate records, alongside communication, confidentiality and risk management. Good documentation is not defensive padding. It helps another practitioner know what changed, what was tried, how the person responded, what remains uncertain and what action is due. It should be readable by the person as well as the team. This draft supports reflection but does not confer competency or replace local requirements.

sections.heading: Communicate for understanding
paragraphs: Use plain language, short explanations and one idea at a time. Explain purpose, expected sensations, likely benefits, material risks, alternatives and the option to pause or decline. Check hearing, vision, language, cognition, literacy and cultural needs; arrange a competent interpreter when required rather than relying on children or untrained relatives. Ask open questions, listen without interruption and reflect back what you heard.

Teach-back checks the explanation, not the patient. Ask, ‘Just so I know I explained it clearly, how will you do this at home and what will make you stop?’ Correct misunderstandings without blame. Shared decisions include values, constraints, uncertainty and review. Respectful communication is a safety control: people are more likely to disclose deterioration or a mistake when they feel heard.

sections.heading: Document reasoning and consent
paragraphs: For assessment or treatment, record consent as a process: what was explained, questions, agreement or refusal, adaptations and whether consent was withdrawn. Document chaperone or supporter arrangements where relevant. Connect findings to a working hypothesis and plan: ‘Observed reduced step clearance after four minutes; reports fatigue; will assess endurance and review medication with prescriber if indicated.’ Avoid unsupported labels, copied-forward errors and ambiguous abbreviations.

If a measure is used, include tool and version, score, conditions, assistance and interpretation. If a planned test was not done, say why. If a decision depends on a missing result, make uncertainty visible. Amend errors according to local policy; do not obscure the original entry. Digital records still require attention to access, privacy, device security and appropriate sharing.

sections.heading: Make handover actionable
paragraphs: A handover should answer: who is the person, what is the current problem, what changed, what are the risks, what has been done, what is needed next, by whom and by when? Use a structured format where your service has one, but do not let a template replace judgement. Highlight mobility assistance, precautions, red flags, equipment, communication needs and restrictions according to local rules.

Share only relevant information with people involved in care, using lawful and secure channels. HCPC standards require confidentiality but permit disclosure with permission, where law allows, in best interests or to protect public safety. Explain sharing when practicable. Confirm receipt for urgent referrals and document unsuccessful attempts and escalation. Clear written or oral instructions are central to physiotherapy safety.

sections.heading: Review quality and repair harm
paragraphs: At review, reconcile the record with experience. If the plan is not working, document the conversation and change rather than silently carrying forward old goals. Invite corrections and respond to complaints respectfully. If something goes wrong, HCPC standards require openness, honesty, appropriate reporting, explanation, apology and corrective action. Follow incident and duty-of-candour procedures; never edit a record to make an event disappear.

Documentation and communication skills develop through feedback, supervision, audit and reflection. Follow local law, retention rules, information governance, professional standards and templates. The standard is not maximal detail; it is a clear, timely, proportionate record that helps the next safe decision and keeps the person involved in it.

sections.heading: Further practice considerations
paragraphs: A concise note can still show depth: subjective report, objective findings, interpretation, plan, consent and safety-net. Avoid copying old findings without checking. Ask what success looks like and what may make the plan difficult. Exercise instructions should include position, dose, acceptable response, stop criteria and how to seek help; ensure written and verbal advice agree.

Ask what success looks like and what may make the plan difficult. Exercise instructions should include position, dose, acceptable response, stop criteria and how to seek help; ensure written and verbal advice agree.

A record should make uncertainty and accountability visible. If an instruction came from another clinician, identify it; if advice was adapted, explain why; if follow-up is contingent, name who owns it. Good notes support audit and learning without turning the person into a collection of codes. Invite the person to correct factual errors and explain how they can raise concerns. Communication remains part of treatment at every review, not an administrative afterthought.

Documentation also supports continuity across settings. Include the person's baseline function, relevant precautions, response to treatment, agreed home programme and the next review condition. When transferring care, distinguish completed actions from tasks still outstanding and identify the responsible professional. Avoid unexplained jargon that can be misunderstood by a patient, family member or colleague outside physiotherapy. Information shared through electronic systems should be accurate, necessary and sent through approved channels. Audit a sample of records for timeliness, clarity, consent, safety-netting and closed-loop referrals, then use findings for supervision and service improvement.

takeaways: Write records that distinguish reported facts, observations, interpretation and plan.
Treat consent and shared decision making as ongoing communication.
Use plain language, teach-back and accessible formats to reduce misunderstanding.
Make referrals and handovers actionable, secure and closed-loop.
